articles.title: Deadly strike on Kyiv warehouse prompts evacuations
articles.excerpt: Nearly 400 people have been evacuated after a Russian strike on a warehouse near Kyiv killed at least 37 people, Ukrainian authorities have said.Videos showing the moment of a huge explosion and the plumes of smoke that followed have been shared online.The strike hit a depot storing weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area.An investigation into the "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosive right next to people" has begun, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson reports.

articles.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
articles.excerpt: A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors. Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle. The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours. Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt. Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.Video produced by Mansi Kapur and Kamal Pariyar. Video edited by Suneth Perera, Jasmin Dyer and Andrew Webb.More on this story here.

articles.title: BBC tracks one week of Israeli settler violence in occupied West Bank
articles.excerpt: Violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank is set to reach record levels this year, as human rights groups warn that they are increasingly spreading into new areas of the territory.Attacks on Palestinians have risen under Israel's current government, alongside a rapid increase in Israeli settlements, illegal under international law.Many of these attacks are not widely reported on.The BBC's Lucy Williamson has been tracking settler attacks on Palestinians, which have been observed over the last week alone.

articles.title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city
articles.excerpt: Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.Tens of thousands of people are living in tented camps around El Obeid. Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesWhile many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children.

articles.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
articles.excerpt: Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.A visitor takes a picture of the platinum and diamond necklace, which dates from 1939 and belonged to Queen Nazli of Egypt, at the Pierres Précieuses exhibition in Paris. Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/GettyIn an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.Queen Nazli of Egypt, right, wearing the necklace at Princess Fawzia’s wedding in Cairo, 1939. Also pictured, from left, are: Queen Farida, King Farouk, Fawzia and Crown Prince Mohammad.

articles.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
articles.excerpt: In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify.

articles.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’
articles.excerpt: The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said.

articles.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs
articles.excerpt: South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.The seized parrot eggs. Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the EnvironmentThe ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said.

articles.title: Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalates
articles.excerpt: Donald Trump and Canada continued a verbal duel on Saturday over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the Ontario premier erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting a video of him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA.Rhetoric over the naming of Lake Ontario is the public face of an escalating trade dispute between the US and its northern neighbor involving a 50% US tariff on Canadian steel and retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa.Trump’s order for the US government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America by Sunday had at least one prominent impact. Google Maps had changed Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America for US users to reflect the president’s executive renaming order.Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney has flat-out rejected the renaming, explaining that Lake Ontario derives from an Indigenous Wendat word meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is great” that dates back more than 400 years.Ontario premier unveils Lake Ontario sign in response to Trump’s ‘Lake America’ order – videoWith talks to resolve the trade dispute stalled, Trump issued an executive order on Thursday directing US agencies that the lake was now Lake America.It revived memories of a dispute earlier in his second presidency with Mexico, which saw Trump direct US agencies to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters before he signed an executive order renaming the body of water among US federal agencies.In a statement explaining why it was acquiescing to Trump’s desired name for Lake Ontario, Google said its practice is to “reflect name changes in official government sources”.

articles.title: Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez defends ‘endless’ benefits of her oil deal with Trump
articles.excerpt: Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has defended her government’s highly controversial energy deal with Donald Trump, insisting the South American country will maintain ownership and sovereignty over its massive oil reserves.Rodríguez, who assumed power in January after Trump ordered the abduction of the president, Nicolás Maduro, took to the airwaves on Saturday to push back against criticism of what the US president has called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.“The benefits are endless,” claimed Rodríguez, a former vice-president whom Trump backed after ordering Maduro’s capture during a special forces raid on the capital, Caracas.During a six-minute television broadcast, Venezuela’s acting leader claimed the deal would help her resource-rich country develop its economy, earn revenues of more than $209bn (£154bn), and become “an energy powerhouse”.Rodríguez said: “As everyone knows, our country has the biggest oil reserves in the world. But having resources underground isn’t enough. We need investment, technology, infrastructure [and] production capacity to convert this wealth into wellbeing for our people.”She added: “It’s no use having our oil reserves underground, only to appear in statistics or bookkeeping … and for us not to be able to convert and translate them into development for Venezuela.”Trump announced the “groundbreaking” deal on Friday, calling it a “historic transaction [that] more than doubles American oil reserves … while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity”.Oil platforms and pumpjacks at Lake Maracaibo in north-western Venezuela.

articles.title: Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?
articles.excerpt: In mid-June, 99 guerrilla fighters were flown by helicopter to a small settlement in a rural area of southern Colombia where they lined up and, one by one, handed their weapons to government officials: rifles, pistols, machine guns and grenade launchers.They also stripped off their heavy tactical vests, field packs and camouflage uniforms, which were each piled into a bonfire to mark the beginning of a new life away from an armed conflict that has claimed nearly half a million lives in the last six decades.That was precisely what the former president Gustavo Petro’s “total peace” plan had sought to achieve: negotiating with and disarming all of Colombia’s criminal groups, which are estimated to have nearly 30,000 members.But the group of just 99 people was the only one to disarm, and did so just three days before the presidential runoff, which was won by the far-right millionaire lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who had campaigned on a promise to end “total peace” and return to a full-on strategy of jailing or killing criminals.Now, several weeks after the new president took office – and amid efforts to deal with the aftermath of the 7.4-magnitude earthquake, as his government has already begun the promised airstrikes against criminal groups – the 99 do not know what will happen to them.“We’re in limbo,” said Natalia Bríñez, 29, one of 13 women among the group staying in the temporary location zone, or ZUT by its Spanish initials, a government-controlled zone where, under surveillance and unable to leave, they were supposed to make the transition to civilian life over the following months.Natalia Briñez, a former guerrilla fighter, is one of 13 women in the ZUT. Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The GuardianThe former guerrillas are housed in beige brick buildings decorated with drawings they painted themselves, including doves of peace, with a communal dining hall where three meals a day are served.

articles.title: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela
articles.excerpt: Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves.The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.The administration, Trump wrote, has “secured majority U.S. control of more ​than 65 BILLION ‌BARRELS of proven Oil ‌Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the ‌American Taxpayer”.Trump said the agreement would more than double American oil reserves.“This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubio wrote on social media.Trump’s announcement provided few details on the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved, or how the US would exercise majority control over the ⁠reserves.Venezuela has an estimated 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves, the world’s largest.Since the US captured and removed former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying ‌to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude oil for US refineries while promoting American investment ​into the Opec country’s deteriorated energy industry, which produces 1.25m barrels per day of crude.Trump is under pressure before November’s midterm elections over rising gasoline prices, ​which could ​be eased through ​cheaper oil supplies and expanded output.The US ​also has ‌been looking ​for solutions ​to replenish its strategic petroleum reserve, the oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers.Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was “in advanced talks with Venezuela for the U.S. to take a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields that house nearly one-third of the country’s massive energy reserves”.

articles.title: Venezuelan opposition up in arms over reports US wants big stake in oil and gas
articles.excerpt: Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s massive energy reserves have sparked an outcry, with critics describing the move as “predatory” and a “rapacious” land grab.Several media outlets this week reported that the Trump administration – which abducted Venezuela’s authoritarian president, Nicolás Maduro, in January and has steered the South American country ever since – hopes to secure long-term access to its oil and gasfields.Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn.On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal said Trump officials were in “advanced talks” with Venezuelan officials to take “a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields” containing 90bn barrels, nearly a third of Venezuela’s energy reserves.“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” a source told Reuters, which said the fields being negotiated were in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.Axios claimed the deal would be “a legacy-defining moment for President Trump”, with one unnamed official telling the US outlet: “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement … It is massive.”Bloomberg, citing sources familiar with the negotiations, said one deal under discussion was a 100-year lease on several oilfields.The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticising the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan.

articles.title: Search continues as number missing in Nepal-Tibet floods rises to 2,478 – as it happened
articles.excerpt: From 2d agoDeath toll now stands at 579 in Nepal, seven in TibetNepal’s official death toll from Wednesday’s flash flood now stands at 579 people, while China says seven people have died in Tibet, the state Xinhua news agency reported early Saturday.Chinese authorities said also they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among those missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash.Sivaranjani Muthunathan was travelling by bus with 56 others to the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam.“Then there was fog, smoke, something that seemed to suddenly engulf us,” Muthunathan, 46, told Agence France-Presse on Friday, showing a phone video she recorded of a torrent surging towards her. Around them, vehicles were swept away or buried under mud.Relatives check the lists of missing people following the flash floods in Nepal, outside a hospital in Kathmandu on Friday.

articles.title: At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross
articles.excerpt: The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, which have killed nearly 600 people, left another 1,900 missing, and triggered a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.“The trauma of this event is enormous,” David Fisher, the IFRC head of delegation for Nepal, said on Friday.“Thousands of homes have been destroyed or suffered significant damage. We believe that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in great need. The death toll is very high and unfortunately likely to continue to rise.”The deadly floods occurred on Wednesday morning after an enormous section ⁠of a glacier in the Himalayas broke loose and crashed on to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, unleashing a massive surge of water, mud, rock and ice that thundered down rivers and valleys. The resulting floods obliterated villages and destroyed power stations, roads and bridges.Map of key locations affected by the flash floodsNepal’s steep slopes and the lush valleys below are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events, such as intense monsoons, and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.“The damage is just incredible,” Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN resident coordinator for Nepal, said on Friday, adding that more than 40 bridges had been destroyed or badly damaged and “over 40km of road completely destroyed”.By Friday afternoon, the death toll stood at 584 people: 579 in Nepal and five across the border in Tibet, China.

articles.title: Families of 33 missing Britons rush to Nepal as fears grow of more floods
articles.excerpt: Families are rushing to Nepal to search for the 33 British nationals who are still missing, as fears mount over the risk of a second wave of flooding in the region.The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and sweeping away entire villages, have killed at least 538 people, while more than 1,500 remain missing.Among them are hundreds of foreign tourists who were visiting the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims for its natural beauty and religious significance.Relatives of missing Britons have shared their devastation as they desperately try to reach their loved ones who were last seen in the Rasuwa district, where power and communication lines are down. Many are scrambling to book flights to Kathmandu, the Nepalese capital. On Friday, authorities in Nepal and China issued warnings about the risk of a second wave of flooding. Chinese authorities said an artificial lake had formed after a mudslide hit the Tibet-Nepal border, posing a risk of “sending flood waters downstream”, according to state media. Nepal’s disaster authority said a lake that had formed after debris blocked a river at the site was also rising and ‌at risk of bursting.Barrier lake forms at base of mountains near Nepal borderRescuers were forced to suspend their search for survivors, while residents who had returned to Rasuwa were told to evacuate their homes. Many were seen fleeing up the hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river.In a video on YouTube, Jaggi Vasudev, known as Sadhguru, a spiritual leader who founded the nonprofit Isha Foundation, told followers at the foundation’s camp at Saga in Tibet, China, that 80 members of an Isha group returning from Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists, were missing, including nine British people.Among them was Neetu Goyal Tiwari, 51. Her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC that completing the pilgrimage was “her dream”.

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at sea
articles.excerpt: The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop in Thailand next week as it heads back to the United States, Thai navy officials said, after spending more than 250 consecutive days at sea supporting US operations against Iran amid recent reports of poor living conditions and low morale onboard the vessel.The Lincoln left the Middle East several days ago after being relieved by the USS George Washington, and is now heading home to San Diego. A Thai navy official told Reuters this week that the carrier was expected to make a brief port visit in Thailand next week for the crew to rest and recuperate before continuing their journey home.“The stop is ‌a ⁠routine port visit intended to allow personnel to rest and recuperate … as well as to receive logistical support,” the spokesperson for the Thai navy said.Earlier this week, the Thai navy said that three ships from a US navy carrier strike group would be making a brief port call in eastern Thailand to allow personnel to rest. No military exercises would take place during the visit, the statement added. The Thai navy did not identify ​the vessels or provide a date.The planned stop comes as the Lincoln’s deployment has faced scrutiny in recent weeks amid reports of poor living conditions onboard among its crew. Family members of sailors have described shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale, and worsening mental health among the roughly 5,000 personnel on the carrier.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet flood rescue efforts resume after being halted by overflowing lake
articles.excerpt: Rescuers searching for survivors of deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have resumed their efforts after suspending operations when a debris dam burst its bank on Friday, increasing the risk of fresh flooding.Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides ⁠on Friday to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses. Fears of another flood came as authorities in Nepal and China said that at least 543 people had been killed in the disaster.Barrier lake forms at base of mountains near Nepal borderMore than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said, including 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.The flood on Wednesday had destroyed power stations, roads and bridges along a route that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet and is ⁠popular with trekkers and pilgrims.The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the China border burst its banks.‘Erased before their eyes’: on the ground in decimated Nepal flood zone - The LatestRescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when a tide of mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday.

articles.title: Australia news live: PM urged to restrict violent pornography after teen’s death; Labor working on release of Oscar Jenkins
articles.excerpt: From 21m agoNSW opposition leader says ‘let’s not wait’ to take action on violent pornographyThe NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, says she has written to Anthony Albanese after a 16-year-old girl died from a suspected sexual strangulation incident.Sloane said the reports were shocking and had “rocked everyone to their core”, saying she had written to the prime minister about the need to tackle violent pornography. double quotation markI’m saying, you know, after the shock of the last week, that let’s act now, let’s not wait any longer. The opposition leader said certain types of pornography should be placed into the most restricted category and pressure should be applied on porn companies and social media giants to “just make sure wherever we’re at, we can block it”. double quotation markIt has the ability to program the young, vulnerable minds of a generation of people whose first sexual experiences are being distorted because of this. Kids at 16, this is shocking. And it’s becoming normalised. Sloane went on to say education about consent was also a critical prong, even if it’s a “very tough” conversation between parents and teenagers. double quotation markIt’s a hard conversation to have with your kids. But around consent, we need to model that behaviour as well. Sloane added that she told Albanese the NSW Liberals were “very supportive” of Chanel Contos’ campaign, Fix Our Feeds, which urges an opt-in mechanism for algorithms. double quotation markThese algorithms prey on people, whether it’s young boys feeding them increasingly misogynistic content online, whether it’s girls preying on their vulnerabilities about their looks and their self-worth. Kellie Sloane.
articles.summary: 新南威尔士州反对党领袖凯莉·斯隆表示，在一名16岁女孩疑似因性窒息事件死亡后，她已致信总理安东尼·阿尔巴尼斯。斯隆表示这些报道令人震惊，"震撼了每个人的内心"，她写信给总理，强调有必要解决暴力色情内容问题。她说："我想说的是，在经历上周的震惊之后，我们现在就要采取行动，不要再等了。"反对党领袖表示，某些类型的色情内容应被列入限制最严格的类别，并向色情公司和社交媒体巨头施压，"确保无论在什么情况下，我们都能屏蔽这些内容"。她还表示："这有能力塑造一代年轻人脆弱的心灵，他们的初次性体验正因此被扭曲。16岁的孩子，这太令人震惊了，而且正在变得常态化。"斯隆接着表示，关于同意的教育也是一个关键方面，即使这是父母与青少年之间"非常艰难"的对话。她说："和孩子谈这个话题很难，但在同意方面，我们也要以身作则。"斯隆补充说，她告诉阿尔巴尼斯，新州自由党"非常支持"香奈儿·康托斯的"修复我们的信息流"运动，该运动主张为算法引入选择性加入机制。她说："这些算法捕食人们——无论是向年轻男孩推送越来越多的厌女内容，还是利用女孩对外貌和自我价值的脆弱心理。"

articles.title: Australian boxing great Tony Mundine dies aged 75
articles.excerpt: Indigenous Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died, aged 75.The father of former boxer and NRL star Anthony Mundine had a heart attack on Sunday.Born in Baryulgil, near Grafton in northern New South Wales, Tony Mundine was the first Australian to fight in four different weight divisions, challenging for the world middleweight title against Argentina’s Carlos Monzon in 1974, in a bout stopped in the seventh round.Tony Mundine with former boxer and activist Rubin ‘Hurricane’ Carter in 2010. Photograph: Lee Besford/AAPMundine leaves a significant boxing legacy. Anthony was an IBO middleweight and WBA super-middleweight world champion, whose son Rahim won his fourth career fight from as many professional bouts on the Gold Coast only last week.Anthony Mundine posted a tribute to his father on social media, saying he was returning home for his funeral after travelling to Saudi Arabia.Anthony Mundine spars with Tony during a training session at his gymnasium in Redfern in 2013. Photograph: AAP“I don’t know what to say, I’m broken,” Anthony posted.“Dad I love you man, may Allah bless your soul.“I’m on my way home to say goodbye one last time till we meet again.NBA star Clyde Drexler with Tony Mundine during a basketball clinic for the Aboriginal community at Mundine's gym in Redfern. Photograph: Tim Cole/AAP“Thanks for doing all you did for me and supporting me in every moment, showing love and strength gonna miss you Tonza, there’s only one Tony Mundine.”Through a career in the middleweight, light-heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight divisions, Tony Mundine recorded 80 wins – 64 from knockouts, 15 losses, and one draw.

articles.title: Cash settlements on home insurance claims leaving vulnerable Australians short-changed, Asic says
articles.excerpt: Home insurers are overwhelmingly paying cash to settle claims, leaving Australians to foot blowouts in repair costs for their cyclone-damaged homes.The corporate regulator is calling for “realistic” bigger payouts, warning the practice could cause “unfair outcomes” for people already in vulnerable positions.In a report released on Monday, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic) found many homeowners were being paid based on a single quote from insurers’ favoured builders.Asic commissioner Alan Kirkland said homeowners were then left to find tradespeople, oversee repairs and pay for unexpected costs and damage, all issues that would otherwise have been handled by insurers.“The easy option for insurers can be the expensive one for homeowners,” Kirkland said.“If the amount falls short, consumers can be left shouldering the cost of repairs and paying the difference out of their own pocket.”A spokesperson for the Insurance Council of Australia said cash settlements could give customers flexibility and control over their own repairs. They said the industry had improved since Cyclone Jasper and focused on ensuring settlements were clearly explained and understood.Asic reviewed a sample of home building insurance claims from Cyclone Jasper, which hit far north Queensland in December 2023.It looked at the companies that it said accounted for most of the home insurance industry: Insurance Australia Group (IAG), AAI, QBE Insurance, Allianz Australia and Sure Insurance.Asic said insurers professed to prefer to settle claims by managing repairs or rebuilding, not by paying cash. The review found none of the five were systematically recording why claims were being settled with cash.Cash settlements were used in more than 63% of final claims.

articles.title: Pacific Islands Forum meeting in turmoil after several leaders pull out of Palau summit
articles.excerpt: Several leaders have pulled out of a the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Palau at the eleventh hour.The Solomon Islands prime minister, Matthew Wale, has cancelled his appearance after a no-confidence motion was lodged against him at home by the Solomon Islands home affairs minister, Manasseh Maelanga.Maelanga accused Wale of “repeatedly making decisions of matters of national importance without proper consultation with, or the approval of, cabinet, thereby undermining the principles of collective cabinet responsibility, representative democracy and good governance”, according to the ABC.Australia has been in negotiations with the Solomons on a security treaty, with the hope that further negotiations could have taken place on the sidelines of the summit.Fiji’s prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, and his Vanuatu counterpart, Jotham Napat, will also not be attending, with the Samoan leader, La’auli Leuatea Schmidt, another notable absence.The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has confirmed he will still be attending.Oliver Nobetau, the Lowy Institute’s Pacific Islands program director, said the pulling out by key leaders “dulls the flame” of the meeting.“This has been shaping up to be quite a significant PIF … it’s really unfortunate that this is the case,” he told Guardian Australia.“With the pulling out of this many key prime ministers within the region, it dilutes the potential of what could come out of this leaders’ meeting.”Nobetau said there were high expectations that this leaders’ meeting could progress pilot projects around Pacific climate resilience, and was important ahead of the Cop31 climate summit in November and a pre-Cop31 summit to be held in Fiji and Tuvalu in October.He added the leaders not showing up could be read as those nations prioritising bilateral agreements with nations including Australia above region-wide commitments.“PIF has to demonstrate its usefulness as well.

articles.title: Renee was at Gyirong Port minutes before flood struck, now her family want to travel from Australia to help search
articles.excerpt: Clair Spry says her sister would hate the attention. She would want it focused on the Nepali people, who have been displaced or are in need of aid. She would want it to be on the impact of the climate crisis, especially on the world’s most economically vulnerable populations.“Her focus right now would not be on her; it would be on the families,” Spry said. “So many people, the Nepalese people, that have been horribly displaced and traumatised. She would want the attention on them and how we are going to help them.“And global warming. This is something the poorest people of the world are affected by. It’s not the New Yorkers, it’s the people who are in these parts of the world. For Renee, that would be heartbreaking.”Renee, an Australian, was travelling in Nepal and is now missing. Photograph: GoFundMeLike many of the missing Australians, Renee arrived at Gyirong Port just 10 minutes before the flood struck. The area was one of the hardest hit – images from Chinese rescue teams show the area completely flattened. Huge buildings, power lines, everything – just wiped away.Renee is a disability support worker who lives on the Sunshine Coast. She has been with her partner, Shaun, an emergency nurse, since they were 15, and they share two daughters in their 20s.Clair has set up a GoFundMe to get the three of them over to Nepal – Shaun wants to travel to the port to try to find any signs of her. And their daughters, Lily and Ruby, don’t want him to go alone.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Their first reaction is, we have to go. The practicalities, and what can actually be done in the first few days, it hasn’t been possible [to enter the area], but they still want to go,” she said.“And if they are able to find her, to bring her home.”A map showing the flood zone in NepalRenee’s family understand how dire the situation is, and how unlikely it is that she, or anyone in that same area, survived.

articles.title: Captain and crew arrested after at least eight die in northern Cyprus ferry disaster – as it happened
articles.excerpt: From 5h agoNorthern Cyprus ferry disaster - key developments so farHere are the main updates from the last few hours: The death toll has risen to “at least 8”, with 18 people still missing. Ünal Üstel, the north’s Turkish Cypriot prime minister, told Turkish state broadcaster TRT that 237 people have so far been rescued. Survivors have described a blast which went off at the vessel’s bow before the catamaran-style ship rolled over. The captain and seven other crew members have been arrested and are in custody The captain was allegedly among the first to abandon ship, according to witnesses who spoke to local media. The boat was sailing from the port of Kyrenia, in the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, to the port of Taşucu in Turkey, when the disaster occurred about 4 nautical miles (7.5km) off the coast. Three children rescued from the sea were in intensive care on Sunday.

articles.title: Jason Arday accuser given three-month teaching ban but can continue research
articles.excerpt: Prof Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas has been barred from teaching on Ghent University campus for three months but has been allowed to continue his research position.Cofnas, an American academic, was suspended from his postdoctoral research position at the Belgian institution earlier this month pending a “preliminary investigation” launched after Arday’s death.Ghent did not name Cofnas but has since confirmed that it has “imposed a disciplinary measure” on a staff member for three months, under which they were “required to work remotely and may not carry out any teaching”. Cofnas’s research activities in the role have been “strictly limited to the research topics for which the appointment was made”.In a post on X, Cofnas said he was grateful to Ghent’s rector, Petra De Sutter, “for allowing me to stay”.The US ambassador to Belgium, Bill White, who had criticised Cofnas’s suspension, claimed on his official X account that the university and Cofnas had “amicably reached an agreement” to lift the suspension, enabling the academic to complete his one-year appointment.In a statement, Ghent said an inquiry was under way “to determine if further disciplinary action is warranted”. The university later confirmed it had been in contact with the US ambassador, who “provided further context regarding his statements on X”.Cofnas’s role at Ghent has been controversial. In May, the university’s philosophy department alleged to the institution’s leaders that Cofnas had “very limited expertise” for his role researching “the future of liberalism” and that he had a “far-right agenda”.In July Cofnas accused Arday, a University of Cambridge sociologist, of plagiarism, alleging also that there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims. Arday was found dead on 14 August.Jason Arday was found dead on 14 August. He was accused of plagiarism by Cofnas.

articles.title: At least eight dead and 18 missing after ferry capsizes off northern Cyprus
articles.excerpt: At least eight people have died and 18 people are missing after a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers and crew capsized off the coast of Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus, local authorities said.The territory’s prime minister, Ünal Üstel, told the state-run TRT news channel on Sunday that 237 people had been rescued. A search was under way for those who remained unaccounted for.“Search and rescue teams are working very intensively to find them,” said the Turkish ​Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhürman. “If there are people still inside the vessel, reaching them does not appear easy ‌at the moment. Efforts are being made using other technologies to reach them as well.”The ferry had “completely sunk to a depth of 514 metres”, said Erhan Arıklı, the territory’s transport minister.The catamaran-style ferry had been travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of divided Cyprus, to the port of Taşucu in Mersin province, Turkey.A screengrab from footage of rescued passengers. Photograph: Reuters TV/ReutersThe port area of Kyrenia is a popular holiday destination for local people ⁠and tourists. The private ferry was one of several daily shuttle services that link northern Cyprus with Turkey.Mehmet Harmancı, the mayor of Turkish-held northern Nicosia, described the disaster as the worst in the more than 40 years since the territory proclaimed independence.“We’ve not seen anything like this before. It’s by far the worst tragedy. There are 23 people still missing. We think most of the passengers were Turks and Turkish Cypriots,” he told the Guardian.Location mapHours after the ferry capsized, many details remained unclear. “We still don’t know how many have been injured or to what degree. All the injured are being brought to hospital here in [northern] Nicosia. I’m off to the hospital and am in the process of gathering warm clothes.”Kyrenia’s mayor, Murat Şenkul, said the ferry belonged to the Filo Denizcilik company and had sunk off Diana beach.

articles.title: Woman, 22, killed and five injured in shooting at Swiss rave
articles.excerpt: A manhunt is under way in Switzerland after a 22-year-old woman was killed ⁠and five people were injured, ⁠some seriously, in a ​shooting at a rave in the northern town of Aarau, local police have said.In the attack in the early hours of Sunday at a techno party at a covered horse-racing track, an Italian woman died from her injuries at the scene, authorities said. All those caught up in the shooting were residents of Switzerland and in their 20s.Police appealed to the public for any images of the incident and said large areas of the town had been cordoned off in the search for one or more attackers.“We have no definite information about who is behind ​the attack,” a police spokesperson, Bernhard Graser, told Reuters. “We don’t know if it’s one, if ‌it’s several people, if they are on ‌the run by vehicle or on foot.”Police officers patrol a street in Aarau on Sunday. Photograph: Michael Buholzer/EPAA 34-year-old witness ‌who asked for anonymity said he heard shots shortly after the music stopped at 2.30am on Sunday, which he initially mistook for fireworks.Some took cover behind a DJ booth and one woman hid behind a refrigerator but was hit in the back by a bullet and bled to death despite efforts to revive her, he said.“It’s just incredibly tragic. She was young,” he said. “That something like this could happen in Aarau, at a local event, ‌is simply unimaginable. I still can’t really process it.”As a precaution police have increased their presence beyond the town – which is about 50km west of Zurich and 30km south of the German border – but Graser said there were indications the shooter or shooters were no longer in the immediate area.Police secure the area around the Schachen racing track after the shooting.

articles.title: Iceland rejects EU accession talks after divisive referendum campaign
articles.excerpt: Voters in Iceland have ⁠rejected ⁠a government proposal ​to reopen ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU after a closely fought referendum campaign that divided the country against a backdrop of global volatility.After a long and anxious night for those on both sides of the debate, the no camp ended up with 52.8% of votes on Sunday morning and the yes camp with 47.2%. Voter turnout was high at 82.5%.The vote was held in the shadow of repeated threats by Donald Trump to invade or acquire neighbouring Greenland. Although Iceland is a Nato member, supporters of EU membership said European solidarity would provide greater protection if Trump ever made similar threats towards the smaller, Arctic island.At a press conference the prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, said the campaign had “raised the debate in Iceland to a higher level” while acknowledging that there were aspects that “could have been done better”.Kristrún Frostadóttir speaks to reporters on Sunday after the result. Photograph: Leonhard Föger/ReutersGiven how close the outcome was, she said, it was important to respect the views of yes voters. But she said: “It is quite clear that this matter will not move forward under this government.”She said the government would wait to decide on whether to submit a parliamentary resolution formally withdrawing its EU membership application.

articles.title: US strikes Iranian launchers in strait of Hormuz, sparking reprisal attack on airbases in Jordan
articles.excerpt: Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month.“I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak island,” a US official said on Sunday.

articles.title: Palestinian woman and NBC News team reportedly attacked in West Bank
articles.excerpt: A Palestinian woman and an NBC News team are reported to have been attacked and injured by masked Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Saturday, amid worsening confrontations in the area.Benjamin Netanyahu said he condemned the violence committed “by a handful of rioters”.The attack occurred when four members of the news team were interviewing Aida Ahmed Abdullah and her family in the Palestinian town of Jalud, near Nablus.Abdullah told the outlet that they had been driven out of their home by settlers, and the team was walking down a hill toward the house.A car with Israeli license plates reversed up the hill toward them. At least four men with their faces covered leapt from the vehicle, hitting them with sticks and throwing rocks.“They jumped out, beat us, then jumped back in the car,” said NBC News correspondent Matt Bradley. Bradley was hit twice in the arm and treated at a nearby clinic.Abdullah, 51, was taken for medical care by the Red Crescent. Her injuries were not life-threatening. Three other members of the news team were also injured and treated.“Suddenly a car came to us,” said producer Lawahez Jabari. “The settlers had sticks, I saw a gun, but they didn’t use the gun.”Camera operator Khaldoon Eid said the team had not expected to be attacked in a village.Several violent incidents in the area were reported on Saturday. Palestinian workers were pepper-sprayed in nearby Qusra by masked Israeli settlers.Israeli security forces told the outlet they had received reports that “violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians”.They said “security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside”, the statement said.“The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside.

articles.title: Bondi library returns book How to Sell a Genocide to shelves after State Library ‘outlines the law’
articles.excerpt: A Sydney library has returned to its borrowing shelves a book critical of Israel called How to Sell a Genocide following a public campaign and an intervention from the State Library of New South Wales.Waverley library removed the book “for review” earlier this month after the Jewish news outlet JWire reported it had approached the council.JWire said a survivor of December’s antisemitic attack at Bondi, during which 15 people were killed, saw How to Sell a Genocide on the “new release / hot item” shelf and wrote on Facebook that the display was distressing for survivors and bereaved families.Guardian Australia was unable to locate the Facebook post. Waverley library at Bondi Junction is in the same council area as Bondi beach.A staff member at the council-operated library on Friday confirmed the book was back on its shelves. Waverley council was contacted for comment.The State Library had written to the council reminding it of its obligations under guidelines issued by the Library Council of NSW and the Library Act “which was amended in 2026 to reinforce their independence to develop and maintain collections”.“The State Library of NSW supports free and equitable access to information,” a spokesperson said.“The library acknowledges that some books and materials may not align with everyone’s personal views, experiences or beliefs, but supports the right of individuals to make their own choices about what they read, view and access.“The library has outlined to Waverley council the law and policy relevant to this situation.”Ramia Abdo Sultan, a lawyer, helped organise a change.org petition calling for the book to be returned to the shelves.

articles.title: Trump downplays Moscow visit by CIA director as ‘semi-routine’
articles.excerpt: Donald Trump has downplayed a visit to Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, as “semi-routine” after he turned up in the Russian capital unannounced, triggering a wave of speculation about the reasons for his trip.Ratcliffe was reported to have flown to Moscow on a government transport plane on Tuesday in a rare visit after taking off from the Andrews air force base in Maryland.The White House, CIA, Pentagon and the US air force all declined to comment on the visit, which was confirmed on Wednesday by the Kremlin spokesperson, Dimitry Peskov.Interviewed by the conservative radio host Glenn Beck, Trump poured cold water on speculation that Ratcliffe had travelled in response to fears that Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, was planning to “test Nato resolve” or to win Moscow’s cooperation for intensified US sanctions on Iran.“None of the above,” the US president said in response to Beck, who referred to the speculation as “crazy”.“He’s there, you know, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump said.“John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He’s the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things that you said. Now something may come … out of it. We’re working very hard to get that war ended, and frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point.”On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the visit, that the reason for the spy chief’s surprise visit was to warn Russia not to attack Nato countries.Ratcliffe’s visit was the first from a CIA director since his predecessor Bill Burns travelled to Moscow in November 2021 to warn Putin of the consequences of attacking Ukraine.The Russian leader went ahead with the attack regardless in February of the following year.

articles.title: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive
articles.excerpt: As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the territory, farmers are using every last remaining patch of unspoiled earth, no matter how tiny, in their struggle to survive.With severe shortages of water, fertiliser and pesticide, and with more than 80% of greenhouses ruined, it has taken inventiveness and determination to clear land of debris and coax new seedlings into life. Moreover, venturing out into the open to tend to plants can be deadly.Saqer Abu Rabee’s eldest son and brother were killed while at work growing food for their communities on their small agricultural plots in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza. His son Yousef was 24 when he was killed by a drone-fired missile in October 2024. Abu Rabee was working in the fields 10 metres from his son when it happened.“The missile was aimed directly at him and I have no doubt that he was the intended target,” Abu Rabee said. Yousef was well known locally as the driving force behind a collective first called We’ll Plant It and now simply Our Land, which brought together volunteers and encouraged farmers to go back to the land to restore agriculture in the area.Yousef at work in 2024. He was killed by a drone-fired missile that year aged 24. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian“They decided to target him directly,” said Abu Rabee, who stressed his son had no political affiliations. “Before his death, we received daily threats from the Israeli army. They shelled our area every day three or four times while I was working alongside the labourers.”Abu Rabee’s brother Bilal was killed on 2 July after he went to retrieve some agricultural supplies from a destroyed building. His death came nine months into a partial ceasefire during which Israeli forces have killed more than 1,200 Palestinians.

articles.title: Nepal Turns to Mass Burials, as Thousands Remain Missing from Floods
articles.excerpt: Only a fraction of the over 2,500 missing are turning up among the dead, underscoring a bleak reality: The death toll is likely to keep rising for days to come.
articles.summary: 尼泊尔洪水灾害导致超过2500人失踪，目前仅少数遗体被发现，当局被迫进行集体埋葬。这一情况凸显出严峻现实：未来数日死亡人数可能持续上升。

articles.title: China Says 261 Foreigners From 23 Countries Are Missing in Tibet Flood

articles.title: Families of pilgrims likely caught in floods are desperate for news from Nepal
articles.excerpt: A young boy is helped by a women to put up a photograph of her missing relative on a wall alongside photographs of missing and deceased people displayed outside a government hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal, Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. Dar Yasin/AP hide caption toggle caption Dar Yasin/AP As the possibility of more mudslides threaten towns along the Nepal-China border, the search continues for more than 2,400 people missing, including dozens of U.S. citizens, after last week's catastrophic floods. Nepal's Ministry of Foreign Affairs Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai said Sunday that 734 bodies have been recovered four days after nearly 30-foot high waves of water swept through mountain valleys. The Red Cross estimated that more than 90,000 people were affected by the flooding. Nepal says it has deployed thousands of rescue workers, with people still being found alive this weekend. As of Sunday morning, 85 Americans are still unaccounted for, according to U.S. State Department Spokesperson Tommy Pigott. "We've also now seen nine Americans be safely evacuated. We are currently unaware of any U.S. citizen deaths at this time," Pigott said during an interview with ABC News "This Week." Among the Americans missing are tourists, hikers and those on a pilgrimage to the holy site of Mount Kailash, which is located in a remote part of the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. It's considered a once-in-a-lifetime journey for several faiths. Divya Chandrashekar told NPR that her brother-in-law Ragu Rajan, and his wife, Archana Suresh, had planned the trip to Mount Kailash for the past year. The couple from Murphy, Tx. started their journey from Kathmandu on Aug. 25 and were crossing the Nepal-China border when the floods hit. Their last known location was near the Gyirong Port border post on the morning of the floods. The Bhote Koshi, the Nepali name for "Tibetan river," completely wiped out the border checkpoint and the Friendship Bridge that connects Nepal and China.

articles.title: Canada claps back at Trump's efforts to rename Lake Ontario as 'Lake America'
articles.excerpt: Ontario Premier Doug Ford, right, and Niagara West Member of Provincial Parliament Sam Oosterhoff unveil a sign for Lake Ontario at the Fifty Point Conservation Area in Grimsby, Ontario, Canada, on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press via AP) Keito Newman/The Canadian Press/AP hide caption toggle caption Keito Newman/The Canadian Press/AP Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a giant billboard on the Canadian shoreline on Saturday, with the message "Lake Ontario — Now and Always," hitting back at President Trump's efforts to rename the lake "Lake America." The sign, written in both English and French, was put up near the U.S. border, along a major road many Americans travel on when visiting Canada. "President Trump can call it whatever he wants, but I can tell you the rest of the world will always call it Lake Ontario," Doug Ford told reporters. "We're resilient and we're strong Canadians who are always going to protect our sovereignty, always, and we'll never ever back down from a bully, ever." Ford echoed Canada's prime minister Mark Carney who last week said in a post on X, "Canadian women and men … know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario — today and forever." President Trump signed an executive order last week directing the federal government to rename the lake, which sits between New York and Canada. It's the latest in his escalating dispute with Canada, and follows a similar move from the president last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico, the Gulf of America. "We have a gulf, and we have a lake, now all we need is an ocean," Trump told reporters at the Oval Office signing. Trump went on to say he was renaming the lake because trade talks with Canada had gone badly. "People — oftentimes they'll ask me, who's the worst to deal with on trade? And I said, that's easy. Canada. They are the worst at trade. And they feel entitled, and just — we can't have that," Trump said.

articles.title: From Appalachia to Africa: Why Dolly Parton was beloved across the continent
articles.excerpt: Nigerian country singer Ochiora Okogeri, popularly known as The Country Man, performs Dolly Parton songs during International Cowboy Day celebrations in Nairobi in July 2026. Luis Tato/AFP via Getty Images hide caption toggle caption Luis Tato/AFP via Getty Images JOHANNESBURG—Dolly Parton was truly a global star, her reach extending from the hills of Appalachia to the savannas of Africa, where she was beloved across the continent—from Lagos to Nairobi to Johannesburg. At the news of her death this week, African country music stars and fans told NPR they could relate to Parton's background and her ballads of rural hardship and struggle. Esther Konkara, a singer known as "the Kenyan Dolly Parton," said that growing up in a semi-arid, dusty Kenyan village, Dolly's songs just spoke to her. "I think by Dolly singing songs about growing up in rural areas back there in America, and a lot of us having grown up in rural areas and in poor backgrounds it resonates so well with us," she explained. "I think that's why there is a lot of love for country music in Kenya," the 39-year-old added. So much so, in fact, that there's now an annual Cowboys and Cowgirls Day festival where Kenyans — and fans from all over — don western garb and dance to country music. Dolly Parton performing in Nashville, Tennessee in 2014. Terry Wyatt/Getty Images hide caption toggle caption Terry Wyatt/Getty Images Elijah Manyeki, who owns a niche but popular Nairobi store selling cowboy apparel, is the event's main organizer. "The whole of Africa, we are in shock, and we can't believe Dolly she's no more," he told NPR, adding that he was holding a candlelight vigil and barbecue in Nairobi for Dolly fans to come together and remember her. That connection isn't unique to Kenya. In Nigeria, Ochiora Okogeri, known by his stage name The Country Man, is also feeling Dolly's loss.

articles.title: Nepal warns of possible fresh flooding as communities grapple with devastation
articles.excerpt: A drone view shows rescue workers inspect the area and damaged structures following recent flash flooding along the Trishuli River in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP hide caption toggle caption Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP DHADING, Nepal — Authorities in Nepal warned of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River. Flood warning notices were sent to people's phones early Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst hit by Wednesday's catastrophic floods, which killed at least 760 people and left more than 3,000 missing in Nepal and Tibet. In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some residents began returning to ruined homes to see what can be salvaged. Residents sat in homes with walls washed away by the floods, shoveling sludge-like mud and rubble off balconies or window frames. Others scanned the ground for items they could pick out of the mud and rinse off. One man had returned for his chickens, which he found alive. He tied them up and put them in the cabin of his truck. "Everything is finished. Nothing is left. Not even our home," Sharmila Tamang, a Dhading resident who was trying to salvage items from her home, told The Associated Press. At a key power plant that was severely damaged by the floods, workers started inspecting the facilities Sunday to survey the destruction. The plant serves over 20,000 people across four districts. In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. Some pointed to enormous rocks washed downriver during the earlier floods, while others standing on a suspension bridge were warned off with whistles.

articles.title: Icelanders vote 'no' to talks aimed at joining the EU in close referendum
articles.excerpt: An election worker assists a voter at a polling station inside Reykjavik City Hall in Reykjavik, Iceland, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. Marco Di Marco/AP hide caption toggle caption Marco Di Marco/AP Voters in the tiny Nordic nation of Iceland decided against resuming talks about the country joining the European Union in a closely contested referendum, results showed Sunday. The vote against the EU won by 52.8 percent, according to RÚV, Iceland's broadcaster. It was not the first time Iceland had considered joining the EU. The government was in talks with the EU in 2013. Iceland had just come out of a banking collapse after the global economic crisis. Talks stalled in part because Icelanders worried they would lose sovereign control over their fisheries, their largest export. Even if the "yes" vote had won, the country would not automatically have become a member of the EU. Negotiations would have had to reopen with Brussels, and if an agreement was reached, there would have had to be a second referendum on whether Iceland should join the economic pact. "This is a good day," Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir told a reporter Saturday, outside a polling station in the capital of Reykjavik. "We have now reached the point where this is in the hands of the nation. Either we enter these negotiations, seek a good agreement and then see what happens, or we put the discussion about the European Union aside, at least for the time being." Frostadóttir has led a pro-EU coalition government since late 2024. In an interview in July with The Rest is Politics, a leading British podcast, she said the country already adheres to 75% of the EU rules. "Joining it is not going to sink the country and joining it is also not fundamentally going to change every aspect of Icelandic, you know, economy," said the prime minister. But many in the country with a population of just 400,000 worried they'll be drowned out by the 27 other nations in the economic pact.
